items.lbText:
Bank of England warns of increases for millions coming off fixed deals over next three years as interest rates rise

More than 400,000 UK homeowners will face a £500-a-month increase in their mortgage payments over the next three years, as rising interest rates heap extra pressure on households, the Bank of England has said.

The Bank’s financial policy committee said on Thursday that out of the 7 million borrowers coming off fixed-rate deals before December 2029, about 6.5 million would have to cough up extra funds to cover their home loan payments.

For about 3.4 million borrowers the monthly increase would be less than £100, while for a further 2.7 million it would be £100-£500. The increase would be even greater for those borrowers coming off much lower interest rates, with about 430,000 likely to see their monthly mortgage payments surge by more than £500.

Warnings about the increases came after policymakers at the Bank of England hiked interest rates from 3.75% to 4% this month. The Bank also hinted at another increase in interest rates to combat inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war. The financial markets have predicted three quarter-point rate rises by summer 2027.

Over the next year, about 1 million households will see their payments rise by almost £200 a month.

The news will put further pressure on Andy Burnham’s efforts to offset cost of living pressures, with the chancellor, John Healey, having used his first budget to promise “breathing space” for hard-pressed consumers .

The figures came a day after the energy regulator for Great Britain raised the cap on household energy bills by 26% .

The Bank’s deputy governor for financial stability, Sarah Breeden, said it was important to keep in mind that households would “face this [mortgage] shock with strong balance sheets”.

She said household debt was relatively low, at a level last seen in the early 2000s. “So they start from a position of some resilience. And secondly … while there’s a distributional effect and some households would be hit more than others, in aggregate we think this is absorbable.”

The Bank also raised concerns on Thursday about cybersecurity and AI threats after recent outages at Google and Microsoft laid bare businesses’ growing dependence on outside technology, and how “disruption at a single provider” could “affect many firms at once”.

The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, told a press conference that policymakers were worried about “open weight” AI – open source models, many of which are being developed in China. “These models can be run more cheaply … Safeguards may be disabled or removed more easily. This could make more advanced AI capabilities more readily available and useful to malicious actors,” he said.

The Bank also raised fears for the first time about emerging quantum computing capabilities potentially undermining the encryption technology that protects essential financial transactions.

Bailey said quantum computing would have been at the top of everyone’s mind this year, but that the surprise development of frontier AI models had overshadowed those concerns.

“It’s slightly moved quantum into the background … as you can see, we are very intentionally saying we can’t forget about quantum computing, it’s still coming down the track,” he said.

He emphasised that it was crucial, and possible, for banks to start to build up their defences against quantum risks, even while the technology was in nascent development. “It could have powers that go beyond what we’re seeing with frontier AI and have substantial power to undermine cryptography,” he said.

The Bank said the evolving risks reinforced the need for “significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience”, adding that banks needed to have credible arrangements to ensure they could bounce back quickly from any disruption and maintain “vital financial services”.

The financial policy committee acknowledged this would place competing demands on lenders’ tech experts and management teams, but added that a failure to take action would “compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications”.

The Bank also announced plans on Thursday to further reduce capital requirements for UK banks, as part of a wider package that it said could unleash an extra £175bn in lending capacity. However, extra funding could end up being used to pay out shareholders and investors.

items.lbText:
Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco , Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as gloves and masks, the investigation alleges.

Exporting broken electrical goods to Africa is illegal under UK waste export rules in almost every circumstance.

Tesco own brand slow cookers, toasters and Crockpot branded slow cookers, including at least one with a Tesco label, were found on the Accra dump.

Tesco said on Thursday it had suspended its third-party electronic waste management providers with immediate effect while it completed a full audit of them and their practices.

“We’re extremely concerned about these claims … We remain committed to removing or reducing the waste across our operations wherever we can and we work closely with experts to ensure we handle materials responsibly, in line with legal requirements and our own robust standards,” the store said.

Argos items including its own brand Cookworks products, slow cookers, toasters and food slicers were found at the dump.

Argos also said it was mounting an investigation into how the items had ended up there.

“As a responsible retailer, we have processes in place for products returned to Argos. We take these findings seriously and are reviewing the information provided to establish what further action is needed to ensure our requirements are met,” Argos said in a statement.

The investigation found dozens more British items bearing returns labels for sale, including many marked as faulty, being sold in secondhand shops in the area.

Shopkeepers said they had bought the items from brokers in the UK, who provided them as mixed shipments of home electrical equipment.

“The percentage of unusable products varies [by shipment] but sometimes it can be about 10%,” one vendor said. “What do I do with the broken ones? I put them in this box and the Agbogbloshie boys come to collect it.”

All major UK retailers who sell electrical goods operate a take-back scheme which requires them to accept and recycle disused items – for example, a shopper who brings in their old toaster when they buy a new one. The goods should be logged as e-waste and contribute to stores meeting their government-mandated recycling targets.

Under the waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) regulations, the goods should be passed on to approved processors. They can only be exported if the shipper can prove they will be handled in high-quality facilities.

No facilities in west Africa are approved to receive British WEEE, according to the Environment Agency .

“Ghana is not a dumping ground for broken appliances or failed retail returns from the UK,” Joshua Awuku-Apaw, a Ghanaian environmental consultant, told Unearthed. “Shipping faulty, non-functional kitchen appliances abroad under the cover of ‘reuse’ or ‘second-hand trade’ shifts the financial, environmental, and health costs of overconsumption on to Ghanaian communities and workers … Ghana’s communities should not bear the health burden of UK retail waste.”

The investigation traced the route by which the products could have ended up in Ghana. When recently bought items are returned to shops for a refund, even when they are being returned because they are faulty, they can enter a separate stream, the liquidation market, along with other consumer returns, the investigation found.

“Just because somebody in the supermarket says it’s not working, doesn’t always mean they’ve technically declared it as waste,” said e-waste expert Mark Sayers.

Many of the items Greenpeace found in Agbogbloshie and second-hand stores had stickers labelling the goods as “untested return”.

The investigation alleged that returned goods are often sold off in bulk, at a fraction of their shop shelf-price. Sometimes this takes place via the retailers’ own stock liquidation channels where pallets of returns, including job lots of small household electricals, are sold.

The lots are bought by “jobbers” – individuals and small businesses who buy the goods by the palletload and set about extracting any value they can – whether by listing items individually on eBay or Vinted, selling them in bargain-bin stores or exporting them.

Jim Puckett, founder of Basel Action Network, which campaigns against the export of e-waste to poorer countries, said that treating untested returns as anything other than waste was a “major loophole”.

“It should be considered waste until proven otherwise,” he said. “Especially if people are buying it at auction or whatever and shipping it all around the world.”

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “Illegal waste exports are a serious crime. There is no excuse for exporting waste to be dumped or landfilled overseas. Waste leaving England must be sent for legitimate recovery or recycling.

“New controls mean exports of waste electrical and electronic equipment must be notified and approved before they leave the country. The Environment Agency is using intelligence to intervene earlier, target suspicious shipments and disrupt the criminals behind illegal waste exports.”

“Anyone who breaks the law risks having shipments stopped, facing prosecution and financial penalties. Waste criminals should be in no doubt, we are watching, we are acting and you will face the consequences.”…

items.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
items.content: <article>The changes could see drivers over 70 stripped of licences if they do not meet standards.</article>
items.lbText:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year , set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail , external .

Drivers over 70 to face eye tests every three years

The NHS provides free eye tests for over 60s, but they are not detailed enough to approve someone to drive.

The BBC understands this system is also being looked at, with the free tests likely to be expanded to become more rigorous.

A Government source said "beefed up measures" were long overdue.

"One life lost on the roads is one too many," they added. "There have been several arguably preventable fatalities on Britain's roads caused by drivers with failing eyesight in recent years.

The DfT said no decision has officially been made on mandating eyesight tests for drivers aged 70 and over.

A spokesperson said: "We recognise the importance of driving for older people's independence but need to balance this with our priority to keep everyone safe on our roads and avoid tragic accidents.

"Mandatory eye tests for drivers over 70 as part of our Road Safety Strategy are one way to do this.

"We are carefully reviewing consultation results," they added. "Older drivers who are fit to drive and have good enough vision have nothing to worry about."

items.title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
items.content: <article>Poundland has collapse into administration. Why?</article>
items.lbText:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland".

She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way".

However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk

Poundland workers 'in limbo' over firm's future

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group, London-based holding company Xyra Group and German investment firm Zachert Private Equity are all also understood to have made offers for Poundland.

Gordon Brothers had also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

Its view was that ultimately breaking the retailer up would provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate would also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale accuse it of driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

Now that the company has entered administration, consultants at Alix Partners have been appointed to pursue a sale of the business and its assets.

There are various options on the table, which include securing a buyer for the business either in whole or piecemeal.

The prime minister has said he wants "every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible".

In the immediate future, Poundland stores and distribution centres will continue operating as normal.

It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical

In the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical

I n the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

The city was renowned for its shipyards, which specialised in building huge teak dhows suitable for long voyages across the Indian Ocean. This craft industry was a pillar of the local economy, contributing to Mandvi’s influence far beyond India, and it continues to employ many families of carpenters and other workers today.

It was from the 19th century onwards that Mandvi began to fall into economic decline. The advent of steamships, the need for deep, modern port infrastructure, and British colonial rule, which restructured maritime trade to serve its own interests, led to a shift in trade to better-equipped ports such as Mumbai.

After independence in 1947, the creation of the nearby port of Kandla definitively marginalised Mandvi commercially. Mandvi was also affected by the 2001 earthquake in Kutch, which damaged some of the old buildings and accelerated its urban transformation.

The city still clings to its few traditional shipyards, where workers from different religious communities build the boats. While a large proportion of them are Muslim, shipbuilding is also part of a very ancient Hindu tradition.

Each dhow takes several years to build by hand and employs about 25 craftsmen. Apprenticeships begin in adolescence, in a world where teams are related and the trade is as much cultural as it is technical.

Away from the shipbuilding, the city today is known for its neglected architectural heritage and its beaches, which attract Indian tourists and middle-class locals.

items.lbText:
Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh in

T he phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.

“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”

Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.

In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia , which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.

On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”

Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.

Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing : “GPU Jesus has risen.”

Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.

Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT . On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”

While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.

The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded : “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.

Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.

Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying : “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”

And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”

Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.

Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.

“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”

Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.

“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.

In a separate statement , Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

items.title: Car finance compensation payments explained
items.content: <article>Millions could be entitled to compensation as a result of commission arrangements between lenders and dealers.</article>
items.lbText:
Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements could face further delays to compensation after the financial regulator said it had made some errors in its calculations.

Driver have already been told they must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement.

Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed.

The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.

Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.

The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.

The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much.

Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.

Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders.

Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement.

The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn.

How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered.

The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme.

Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything.

The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company.

The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts.

Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation .

The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external .

lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge

those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster

some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026

some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014

there are exemptions , external , and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation

those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed

those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim

Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees.

FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers.

Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027.

But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme.

The watchdog has now said it uncovered some mistakes in how it categorised a small group of loan agreements under its redress scheme, which could have a small impact on compensation levels.

"While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects the ongoing litigation," the FCA said. That could leave average payouts somewhere between £819 and £839.

"We will discuss with the challengers and the court the impact on this deadline, and for the timeline of the litigation."

Consumer Voice has said the scheme leaves "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance.

The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.

It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes.

The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme. Without a scheme in place, the FCA has estimated that up to 19 million complaints would need to be handled individually, taking three years and costing lenders £6bn more.…

items.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
items.content: <article>The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.</article>
items.lbText:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

items.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
items.content: <article>The discount chain has fallen into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer.</article>
items.lbText:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The discount retailer formally entered administration on Wednesday afternoon, just weeks before Christmas.

Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal for the business, but no transaction was reached.

This led to Poundland's boss filing for administration, with consultancy Alix Partners appointed to oversee the process.

Alix Partners will pursue a sale of the business and its assets, with Poundland likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.

The administrators said it would look at "all options" for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".

"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

During the administration process, Poundland shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade.

Its owner Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.

Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.

But critical insiders have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.

Mark Newton-Jones, Gordon Brothers' senior EMEA managing director, has been called to appear before a committee of MPs to give assurances that the firm will not act to liquidate Poundland's stock or act in the insolvency process.

Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.

Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board of directors had "taken the difficult decision to appoint administrators" as a result of a deal not being agreed for the business.

"It is with sincere sadness and intense regret that we have to tell you that we had no alternative but to take this decision," he said.

He said owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.

Despite the board's "positive engagement with prospective bidders", Gordon Brothers had told the board there was "no prospect of an acceptable solvent offer" so the owner would no longer extend loans to the business," Williams said.

"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern."

Previously Williams had said that the business was making a "strong recovery".

However, Gordon Brothers' position has been in stark contrast to this.

Gordon Brothers said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability".

A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues".

It said it had stepped in to take over the firm in 2025 when it was struggling, when "no one else was willing to finance the business".

One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year.

Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m.

Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.

Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030. This was rejected.

Gordon Brothers also rejected a deal from the London-based Xyra group, which offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.

A German investment firm, Zachert Private Equity, is also understood to have made a late offer, but that too was rejected.

The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations.

This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.

items.lbText:
The sector is in retreat across parts of the county, with developments paused. Despite a grim outlook for 2027 there is some cause for hope

A shopping centre in London that was due to be knocked down and replaced with a retail emporium and more than 1,000 apartments has been paused , dealing another blow to the government’s housing targets.

Lewisham council’s Green administration, which swept into power in May, insisted a larger number of affordable homes should be included in plans agreed last year with Labour officials.

Landsec, which owns the 1980s red-brick shopping centre in the borough’s town centre, said last month that the council’s demand, combined with “exceptionally challenging economic conditions”, had forced a rethink.

For London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, the lack of progress in the capital’s south-east corner raises alarm bells as he tries to lift homebuilding across the city.

According to Damien Sharkey, the managing director of Hub, a mid-sized UK urban property developer with much of its work in London , the outlook for 2027 is “one of the most challenging in the firm’s 15-year history”.

After a collapse in housing starts to just 4,100 across London in 2025, figures have improved, with 16,290 homes registered in the year to the end of June 2026.

However, this impressive 298% year-on-year growth spurt only takes the capital back to where it was in 2023-24, and well below the 21,660 starts in 2022-23.

Khan’s efforts are not helped by a building safety levy on developers, expected to raise £3.4bn over 10 years, combined with extra regulations governing how to build and insulate tower blocks after the 2017 Grenfell Tower disaster .

The consultants Molior has calculated that housebuilding in London’s private housing sector has fallen by 84% since 2015, despite the capital needing 88,000 new homes annually.

Housebuilding has also been in retreat in some other parts of the country – in the West Midlands, completions fell 7% in the year to June, while in north-west England they were 4% lower.

On Wednesday, the property and land development group Henry Boot said its performance this year would be “significantly below current market expectations”. Shares in the company, which builds homes mainly in the north of England,plunged by 20% to a 13-year low as it predicted it would make an underlying loss of up to £10m this year, blaming weak consumer and business confidence.

“In theory, Yorkshire-based property and land developer and housebuilder Henry Boot should be a beneficiary of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s growth and levelling-up agendas, but the shares are getting flattened after a third profit warning this year,” says Russ Mould, the investment director at the platform AJ Bell.

“A weak housing market means housebuilders are cutting their purchases of land and Henry Boot, like Crest Nicholson earlier in the week, is also warning of both weak demand at its housebuilding business and the need to review the value of the land bank on its balance sheet,” Mould added.

Figures from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) show a decline in “new-build dwelling completions” in England from almost 43,000 in the second quarter of 2024 to below 36,000 in the same period this year. Annually, completions fell from about 212,000 in 2022-23 to 190,000 in 2024-25.

The weak housing market will dent the housing secretary Angela Rayner’s target of building 1.5m homes during this parliament, Most analysts believe is it is going to be about 500,000 short by the deadline in 2029.

Glenigan, a construction sector data provider, that charts the rise and fall of developments worth under £100m, says the outlook is grim after a steep decrease in the number of private-sector housing starts in the last year.

Allan Willen, the chief economist at Glenigan, says the private construction sector as a whole, including housing, infrastructure and commercial office building, has suffered over the last year.

“Build costs are high, lending has tightened and demand has softened in some sectors. As a result, numerous projects have been redesigned, delayed or cancelled.”

Those tough conditions are driving more building firms to the wall. About 3,800 firms in the construction sector went into insolvency in the last 12 months , more than any other UK industry sector.

While construction activity makes up only 6% of the economy, a decline in the wider property industry can have a devastating effect on the UK’s growth prospects. According to the latest quarterly figures, the building industry contracted by 0.7% in the three months to the end of September, holding back a rebound in the broader economy that still managed to expand by 0.7%.

Officially, the government’s 1.5m target is still in place, but a succession of profit warnings from big construction groups shows a difficult 2026 for the private sector, which is relied on for 60% of new-build home buildings, will continue next year.

The share price of Britain’s largest housebuilder, Barratt Redrow, has slumped from above 500p for much of 2024 to just 317p this week. Persimmon also suffered a drop in value after the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, followed by a slow recovery that still stops well short of values seen last year.

Reporting an annual loss of between £30m and £40m over the last year, Crest Nicholson has said this week it is struggling with a combination of costly remedial work on some sites and a slump in margins on new ones.

Meanwhile, Taylor Wimpey has cut its profit forecasts and said an industry-wide sales slowdown is in full swing and would “persist well into next year”.

Emily Williams, the director of residential research at the estate agents Savills, says a big issue facing housebuilders is a decline in prices, which she predicts will fall on average by 1.5% next year after zero growth in 2026.…

items.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
items.content: <article>The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.</article>
items.lbText:
The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.

Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

items.title: Guitar wars - the transatlantic battle over the Stratocaster
items.content: <article>US company Fender is in dispute with a German firm that makes generic versions of its key model.</article>
items.lbText:
Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments.

Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton.

The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments.

The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria.

The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954.

In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars.

Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.

Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music.

These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute.

When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers.

The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design.

But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in Düsseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection , external of the Stratocaster design in Germany.

The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The Düsseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections.

The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author".

It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms".

On its website, Fender announced in March , external the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced".

Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe.

One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products".

The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars.

The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians.

"Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments.

Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole.

"We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action."

"For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions."

In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier.

"As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action."

In June, Thomann the company started legal action against Fender, filing an "action of non-infringement" that said that Fender does not have a valid copyright claim to the Stat shape.

Thomann says that the Düsseldorf ruling was simply a default judgement based on missed deadlines and didn't represent a "comprehensive review of the legal claims".

For its part, Fender, which is majority-owned by Hawaii-based company Servco Pacific, says it has a responsibility to protect the Stratocaster's iconic design. In July, it sued Thomann in a German court, for copyright infringement.

In a statement to the BBC, Fender said it remained "confident" in the original Düsseldorf court judgement.

"Our preference has always been to keep lines of communication open and resolve these matters through constructive dialogue rather than litigation," it added.

With the legal cases continuing, Thomann says he believes it is important to get "legal clarity – not only for us but for the wider guitar industry."

"Ultimately, we want to help preserve an environment in which innovation, diversity and creative development can continue to thrive," he adds.

Thomann says he was taking legal action not just for his company, but for smaller music companies too.

"We used to be a small music shop ourselves," he says.

"Many of the smaller manufacturers, guitar makers and dealers affected simply don't have the financial and legal resources to conduct a legal dispute like this."

One such company is LSL Instruments, a family-owned boutique guitar maker in California. Its director of sales, Johny Miller, told me that when they first received Fender's letter they were "pretty terrified and blown away".

"They were asking us to retrieve guitars from dealers out there and destroy them and send them proof.…

items.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
items.content: <article>All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.</article>
items.lbText:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

All three main US stock market indices were down, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq shedding almost 4%.

The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.

Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.

The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.

The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.

Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away

Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.

Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased.

Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by more than 5%.

The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

“I’m looking at the off-peak rate more than doubling, peak increasing considerably as well as the standing charge,” says Andy, who lives on Scotland’s west coast.

“I have an electric vehicle and an air-source heat pump and use a lot of off-peak energy. I’d like to stay with Octopus Energy … but there are better-looking deals out there.”

The retired woodworker is among the millions facing a jump in energy bills when the price cap in Great Britain rises by 26% in January. He says he “got lucky” last time with a “very good” 12-month deal, but it ends next month.

The new cap, set by the regulator Ofgem , works out at £2,166 for a typical annual gas and electricity bill – up £443 on the October to December equivalent. Yet, even though there are dozens of deals available to fix for less, two-thirds of households remain on the default tariff that tracks the cap.

So what is stopping people from switching? We asked for people’s views on why they plan to change provider or stick with a variable account.

For Andy, a big concern is locking in at the top of the market. He has switched numerous times to save money but with variable tracker rates “eye-wateringly high”, he says he worries “that if I fix now at an increased rate, prices could start to come down”.

The cheapest current fix is Fuse Energy’s 18-month deal at £1,754, according to the price comparison service Uswitch. That is £412 a year below the new cap, while the 10 cheapest deals are all at least £317 below it, according to Sabrina Hoque of Uswitch. Its data shows 41 deals are priced below the Ofgem rate.

Opting for a fixed deal is a “way to take control”, Hoque argues. “With only a 1% fall [in the cap] forecast for April, waiting is unlikely to bring much relief, and a fix also protects you from any further rise.”

However, if you are already on a fixed tariff contract with 50 or more days left until it ends you may have to pay an exit fee if you want to switch. The size of this charge varies by supplier and length of deal. They can be as much as £100 per fuel - so if you’re on a gas and electricity deal, it could cost you £200 to leave early.

Hailey, who is a London-based university administrator, has trawled price comparison sites but found that “all the notably cheaper tariffs came from providers I’d never heard of with terrible customer satisfaction ratings”.

“Ultimately, the savings on offer weren’t enough to justify the risk,” says the 36-year-old, who also has an account with Octopus, the UK’s largest supplier with more than 8 million customers. “My provider is reliable, and energy is too important to chase a great offer that might turn out to be too good to be true.

“The prices are getting all but impossible to manage, especially as someone living and paying for bills alone. But I really don’t see what I can do except cut back in other areas, because you’ve got to have light, heat, and electricity for appliances.”

Steve from Merseyside feels there is little point shopping around for a different deal because there “really isn’t much competition any more. They pretty much all charge whatever the cap is.”

The father of two, who works in education, says: “I don’t see that the government has customers’ needs first and foremost with these price increases. They are looking after the energy giants’ profits. ”

There are certainly fewer energy providers – and deals – to choose from than a couple of years ago. The rise in global gas prices caused about 30 small energy suppliers to go bust during late 2021 and early 2022, including Bulb. The number of suppliers in the domestic gas and electricity retail market has fallen from about 70 before the crisis to just 17 today.

Annette, who is in her 40s and lives in Edinburgh, is “stuck” on a variable tariff. “I can’t switch because I’m in a precarious job where I can’t commit to a two-year contract as is usually required. I will likely have to move.”

She says that “paying sky-high rent” is crippling her ability to save: “I already don’t turn the heating on – in Edinburgh. It’s a miserable way to live.”

To help households cope with their energy bills this winter, the government will make a one-off payment of £100 in January to 20m households in council tax bands A to D. The 5% VAT levy has also been taken off electricity bills until July next year.

Rich from Gloucestershire thinks this is not enough. He says: “I remain hugely disappointed that the regulator seems not to be working on behalf of consumers, and that the government is tweaking rather than making the changes necessary to decouple electricity prices from gas , and challenge the profits of the suppliers.”

Rather than fix at a time when wholesale costs are high, Plymouth-based Nick plans to stay on his “no frills” variable tariff with Home Energy, having switched from Octopus.

“We’re planning on riding out the increase in January,” says the 52-year-old telecoms product manager who describes himself as “ultra cautious and tight-fisted by nature”.

“Octopus has a far more attractive user experience and the usage stats are handy, but ultimately it’s all about the tariff rate,” he adds.

“We’ll be OK. We’ll try to be even more energy conscious, but overall we’re counting ourselves to be fortunate enough to be able to absorb the increase.”

People can borrow up to six times their income, but brokers sound alarm over risks of negative equity if house prices fall

A mortgage deal that lets first-time buyers borrow 99% of a property’s value has prompted warnings that even a small dip in house prices could result in borrowers falling into negative equity.

On Wednesday, Nationwide unveiled a mortgage enabling people to buy a home with just a 1% deposit and potentially borrow up to six times their income.

Britain’s biggest building society said it was putting £1bn a year behind the new product, which it believes will open up home ownership to more than 5,000 additional first-time buyers each year.

During the last couple of years, a number of mortgages have gone on sale that require only a small deposit, or no deposit at all. Nationwide said its 99% home loan would “combine meaningful support with responsible lending” – but the mortgage’s launch coincided with data suggesting UK house prices were falling amid the continuing challenging economic conditions.

Lloyds bank said UK house prices dropped by 0.6% in October and were down 1.2% year on year, while the property firm Savills said this month that average prices were expected to drift lower during the rest of 2026 and fall by 1.5% in 2027 .

The Nationwide product is a five-year fixed-rate deal with an interest rate of 5.99%. While many commentators have welcomed it as a lifeline to struggling first-time buyers, some brokers cautioned borrowers could be pushed into negative equity if prices did fall. Negative equity is when someone is living in a property worth less than their mortgage.

Negative equity can leave homeowners trapped, unable to climb the housing ladder as their homes reduce in value.

Riz Malik, an independent financial adviser at the firm R3 Wealth, said: “Nationwide is sticking its neck out with a 1% deposit deal, as even a small slip in prices could leave borrowers in negative equity.”

Darryl Dhoffer, the founder of the brokerage firm The Mortgage Geezer, said those signing up “must tread carefully”. He added: “Borrowing up to six times income at a 5.99% rate creates massive monthly commitments and leaves almost zero equity buffer – meaning even a slight market dip could trigger negative equity.”

Negative equity mainly becomes a problem when homeowners intend to sell their property. As a result, the Nationwide deal was probably most suitable for those buyers “planning to stay put well beyond five years”, said Craig Fish, the managing director of the broker Lodestone Mortgages .

He added: “This is a genuine step forward for first-time buyers who can afford the monthly payments but can’t save a deposit while paying rent.”

Henry Jordan, Nationwide’s group director of mortgages, said “a range of controls” were built into the product to reduce the risk of negative equity.

The deal is only available as a five-year fix, providing certainty over monthly payments, and is restricted to “used” houses only meaning it will not be available to those buying a flat or a newbuild home.

In addition, every applicant must receive mortgage advice and “robust” affordability checks will be carried out, with minimum income requirements imposed and the exclusion of self-employed people.

Jordan added: “I don’t think anyone is forecasting a fall in house prices over the next five years.”

Savills said it expected UK house prices to rise by 15.8% – or £56,500 on average – over the five years to 2031, adding that price growth was expected to accelerate during the second half of 2028.

items.lbText:
Americans are opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or swapping expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives

Thanksgiving is just one day away, but for some Americans, the holiday may look a little different this year as higher costs for food, drinks , household goods, air travel and gasoline have prompted some families to rethink their plans and spending.

The Guardian recently asked readers across the United States how they were marking the holiday this year and whether higher prices had affected their plans or made them rethink their usual traditions.

While some said their plans remained unchanged, many said that they were scaling back and cutting costs. Some said that they were opting for smaller gatherings, reconsidering travel or choosing not to host at all. Others said they were swapping more expensive ingredients for cheaper alternatives or cooking less than they normally would.

In Florida, one man in his 60s said that he and his girlfriend were “scaling way back” this year.

“The expense has made it impossible for us to have what we usually do,” he said, adding that “food is horribly expensive”.

Instead of doing three different pies, they are preparing just one this year, along with a single side dish.

Cindy Van Vreede, 66, in Wisconsin, told the Guardian that the senior center where she goes for “free meals several times a week, is offering to bring a free Thanksgiving dinner to me at my home”.

“By not traveling or expected to bring a dish, I am saving money staying at home,” she said. “I’m also saving money on gas because I’m not driving my car two hours each way.”

A recent report from the American Farm Bureau Federation estimated that Americans preparing a Thanksgiving meal will face “higher prices overall this year”, with the average cost of a 10-person dinner up 6% from last year. It marks the first time since 2022 that American shoppers will see an increase “in the price of goods for Thanksgiving dinner”, according to the report.

The increase for this year is “largely driven by increased prices for Thanksgiving staples such as turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries”, the report says, noting the increases “aren’t a complete surprise as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the supply chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers”.

America’s farmers and ranchers, the report states, are also facing “significant challenges, with record diesel costs, elevated fertilizer prices, increased labor expenses, and a bigger bill for items like rent and electricity – all of which hurt their ability to break even at the end of the year”.

In Texas, 55-year-old Cheryl said that she was “probably not going to celebrate this year”.

“I’ll miss it, just getting together with my family,” she said, “but we can’t afford the food, and going to a friend’s house is unlikely, too.”

Cheryl said that she had watched as her “regular weekly groceries have gone up so much it’s getting harder to afford them”.

Others are finding ways to preserve some of their traditions while spending less.

In Virginia, 39-year-old Hannah told the Guardian: “We’re going low-key.”

“This year, I’m sticking with a few essential dishes – turkey, gravy, potatoes, cranberries, and mac and cheese,” she said. “I’m using recipes that use cheaper ingredients. I’m having my 10-year-old make Kraft mac and cheese from the box rather than using a homemade recipe with more expensive cheeses.”

Hannah said that she was spending “more time than ever looking at prices at different stores, and I’ve been using store loyalty programs to squeeze extra savings”.

A recent survey by Lending Tree found that, among those planning to celebrate Thanksgiving, more than half said that inflation was affecting their plans or budget, with 25% saying that they were changing their food choices as a result, 22% saying they were using more coupons and 14% saying they were cutting back on guests.

The survey also found that nearly two-thirds of respondents said that they may need to borrow to host Thanksgiving, including 38% who said they planned to use credit cards to cover the costs.

In Seattle, Liliya said that she was trying to persuade her partner “not to order the whole turkey but to buy a few cuts instead”.

Their Thanksgiving, she said, “will be a very small family gathering, no different from other years outside of me trying to scale down on the turkey”.

For others, the expense of traveling for the holiday has prompted a change of plans. A woman in North Carolina said that she had decided not to travel this year, partly due to the cost of “fuel and lodging”.

Instead, she said, they will be treating themselves to a restaurant meal.
